title: Japanese Web Novels: Media History, Platform, and Narrative
abstract: Japanese web novels grew into a major segment of the literary market through platforms that judge work by audience response. This article traces the medium’s history, explains the economics of online publishing, and uses isekai (異世界) to show how fiction on these platforms can combine original storytelling with familiar narrative conventions. It closes by situating the Japanese case alongside other East Asian web-novel industries.

title: Multiculturalism between Ideology and Practice: Immigrant Self-Narrations of Community Activism in Toyota, Japan
abstract: Drawing on life-history interviews with three Brazilian community activists in Homi Danchi (保見団地), the article examines how Japan’s official language of multicultural coexistence (多文化共生) takes on meaning in local practice. The activists use that language to build a community around shared work, even as their organizing leaves some residents outside it. The analysis uses Pierre Bourdieu to connect the way people narrate their lives with the way they experience belonging.

title: The Limits of Humanism: On the Discursive Construction of the Japanese Chinatown
abstract: This article uses Jacques Lacan’s theory of discourse to examine how activists and scholars describe Japanese Chinatowns. It compares calls to recognize a distinct community with scholarly efforts to judge the authenticity of Chinatowns. Through the case of Yokohama (横浜), it asks how these accounts relate to the neighborhood’s development as a tourist destination and to the economic interests invested in its image.

title: Western Elegance, Yokohama Style: College Fashion, Urban Redevelopment, and the Rise of Feminine Motomachi in Post-1970 Japan
abstract: This history of Yokohama’s Motomachi (横浜元町) shopping street follows young women readers of fashion magazines, city planners, and local merchants from the late 1970s. It traces how their interests converged in Hamatora (ハマトラ) fashion and in a redevelopment program that made heritage commercially valuable. Reading fashion and architecture alongside planning records, the article recovers the gendered politics of local history and neoliberal urban change.

title: A Lesson in Port Citizenship: Regimes of Historicity in Maritime Museums in Yokohama, Japan, 1961–2022
journal: História da Historiografia: International Journal of Theory and History of Historiography
abstract: Three successive maritime museums communicated changing ideas of civic identity in postwar Yokohama (横浜). Through exhibitions, museum architecture, and fieldwork, this article traces their movement from an emphasis on universal science to romantic visions of the future and then to nostalgia. François Hartog’s concept of regimes of historicity helps explain what those different ways of organizing time meant for local identity.

title: Fantasies of Europe, Fantasies of Japan: Isekai and the Narrative Logic of Japanese Occidentalism
journal: East Asian Journal of Popular Culture
abstract: In popular isekai (異世界) fiction, a Japanese protagonist enters a world imagined as medieval Europe and uses new powers to reshape it. Through close readings of The Familiar of Zero (ゼロの使い魔) and Re:Zero (Re:ゼロから始める異世界生活), this article shows how such stories construct Europe as backward while imagining a Japan entitled to bring modernity back to the West.

title: Global History in Two Chronotopes: Time, Identity, and the Practical Past in Nagasaki, Japan, 1990 and 2006
abstract: Nagasaki (長崎) drew on its history as a maritime trading hub in two expositions held in 1990 and 2006. The first staged a journey across distinct past and future zones, while the second took visitors on walks through the city’s living heritage. The article compares those ways of organizing space and time to show how communities use and contest the past amid economic change.

title: The Politics of Curating Japonisme: International Art Exhibition and Soft Power in Contemporary Japanese Cultural Diplomacy
abstract: The Japanese government organized Japonismes 2018 in Paris to introduce audiences to Japanese culture. This article traces the event’s planning and curation, asking how exhibitions linked prehistoric pottery to contemporary comics and animation through the idea of a timeless Japanese aesthetic. It shows how Japanese cultural diplomacy adapted older Western ideas about Japan to serve economic and political ends.
